DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

The study is clearly structured and most of the arithmetic checks out. However, its three main conclusions do not hold up:

- the service can be rolled out uniformly,
- 1,800 tonnes of treatment capacity at Brookfield is adequate,
- the service is fully funded.

The problems come from a misreading of the pilot data and from a capacity gap the study mentions but never deals with. **I'd recommend not putting it to Cabinet in its current form.**

## Critical issues

**1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types.**
Table 1 shows 66% participation for houses and 21% for flats, more than three times lower. Flats also produced less per participating household (1.4 kg vs 1.9 kg). The data supports the opposite of the study's conclusion: flats need a different approach, such as communal bins, a different caddy size, or targeted engagement. The case for a uniform rollout in Sections 2 and 7 should be withdrawn or rewritten.

**2. The projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the data.**
Section 3 applies a 64% rate. The pilot's overall rate was 57% (Table 1), and 64% matches no row. The 3,290 tonnes is correctly calculated *from* 64%, so the input is wrong, not the arithmetic.

Applying the pilot rates to the district mix (52,000 households, 20% flats) gives:

| | Households | Participation | kg/wk | Tonnes/yr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about 13% below the stated figure. The "All" row's 1.9 kg is also a rounding of about 1.86 kg.

**3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage, and the gap is unaddressed.**
Brookfield offers 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029. Even the corrected projection of about 2,870 tonnes leaves roughly 1,070 tonnes a year (about 37%) with no confirmed destination for at least two years. On the study's own figure, the gap is about 1,490 tonnes.

The only alternative mentioned is a plant 46 miles away, with no gate fee, haulage cost, vehicle-time impact or capacity confirmation. The study needs a costed plan for the excess, for example:
- a second contract,
- bulking and onward haulage,
- confirmation of whether Brookfield's 2029 expansion could be brought forward.

**4. "Fully funded" is not supported.**
- Using the corrected tonnage, the disposal saving falls from £243,000 to about £212,500 (2,870 t × £74). Net cost rises to about £521,000, which already exceeds the £520,000 allocation.
- Only 1,800 tonnes are guaranteed the £74/t saving (about £133,000). Diverting the remaining tonnage to the 46-mile plant will add haulage and possibly a higher gate fee, increasing the shortfall further.
- The £520,000 is described as "provisional" and only "indicated" by Government. The study should state its status, duration, and the Council's exposure if it is reduced or time-limited.
- Depreciation is not cash. The £990,000 vehicle purchase is needed upfront (order by December 2026), and the study doesn't say how it will be financed (capital budget, borrowing, or capital new-burdens funding). If borrowed, financing costs are missing from Table 2.

## Other points to address

- **Staff costs:** £34,000 per operative looks like salary only. Employer NI and pension usually add 20–30%, so if on-costs are excluded, crew costs could be roughly £80,000–£120,000 higher. Holiday and sickness cover (agency or relief staff) isn't included either.
- **Fleet sizing:** There's no rationale for six vehicles: no round modelling, households per round, or tipping trips. The 14-mile run to Brookfield, and possibly 46 miles for overflow, will affect round capacity. There's also no spare or reserve vehicle for breakdowns and servicing.
- **Pilot representativeness:** Six months may capture early enthusiasm, and participation often drops after launch. A sensitivity analysis (e.g. ±10 points on participation) would show how robust the costs and capacity needs are. The 81% satisfaction figure should give the survey sample size and response rate.
- **Statutory deadline:** The Simpler Recycling requirement for weekly household food waste collections applied from 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements only for some authorities. The study should state Thornbury's position: whether a transitional arrangement applies, and whether April 2027 is compliant or already late. This affects both the risk and the urgency.
- **Liners:** Only a three-month supply is mentioned. The study should say whether liners will be supplied on an ongoing basis, since this affects both cost and participation.
- **Possible upside not counted:** Lower residual tonnage could allow residual collection round savings, or support a later move to less frequent residual collection. This is worth noting, even if it isn't relied upon.

## Figures that check out
- Houses 66%, flats 21% and overall 57% are calculated correctly from the household counts.
- Vehicle depreciation: £990,000 ÷ 7 ≈ £141,400.
- Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000.
- Table 2 total: £733,400.
- £74/t × 3,290 t ≈ £243,000, and the net cost of about £490,000, are correct given the study's (flawed) tonnage.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet
1. Remove the "broadly similar" claim and add a specific approach and budget for flats.
2. Recalculate tonnage from the actual pilot rates by housing type, with a sensitivity range.
3. Secure and cost treatment for the tonnage above 1,800 t until 2029.
4. Restate the financial position with corrected savings, staff on-costs, overflow haulage, capital financing and funding risk. Replace "fully funded" with an honest net position.
5. Set out the statutory compliance position and the fleet sizing basis.
